This demonstrates the whole-device scheduling constraint before fractioning is installed. On multi-GPU nodes, adapt this baseline and verify that both fractional workloads use the same GPU.

Measured baseline result

NAME          READY   STATUS    NODE
whole-gpu-a   1/1     Running   <gpu-node>
whole-gpu-b   0/1     Pending   <none>

The script checks this state and removes both baseline Pods.

Step 7: Install KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator

Run the following command to install KAI Scheduler, which includes GPU Fractioning Operator:

./run.sh install-kai

The pinned KAI Scheduler 0.18.5 chart includes GPU Fractioning Operator 0.1.7. The values turn on NvFractions and per-Pod metrics while retaining GPU-stack version checks. The optional nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode annotation selects compute mode. These workloads leave the default unchanged.

Relevant fields from helm/kai-values.yaml

global:
  gpuSharingMode: NvFractions
  nvFractions:
    set: true
gpu-fractioning:
  metricsAgent:
    enabled: true
  skipGpuStackVersionChecks: false

In the validation, FractiondReady, MpsdReady, and Ready are True. DriverUpgradeInProgress is False with reason NoDriverUpgrade, consistent with the AMI retaining driver ownership.

Step 8: Run the positive sharing test

Run the following command to deploy two Pods with 8 GiB GPU-memory contracts:

./run.sh share

Each Pod requests and limits memory to 8 GiB and selects kai-scheduler. Neither requests a whole nvidia.com/gpu resource. The repository applies these scheduling fields and runs a CUDA probe that allocates 6 GiB:

Essential fields from kubernetes/fraction-8gi-pods.yaml

metadata:
  annotations:
    nvidia.com/container.gpu-workload.gpu-memory.request: 8Gi
    nvidia.com/container.gpu-workload.gpu-memory.limit: 8Gi
spec:
  schedulerName: kai-scheduler
  runtimeClassName: nvidia

Measured positive result

NAME             READY   STATUS    NODE
fraction-8gi-a   1/1     Running   <same-gpu-node>
fraction-8gi-b   1/1     Running   <same-gpu-node>

The script verifies matching node names and GPU UUIDs. In the validation, both Pods see 8,192 MiB and report allocation_succeeded_mib=6144. Those checks establish placement on one physical GPU, the bounded device view, and successful allocations within each contract.

Measured allocation output from each Pod

NVIDIA_GPU_MEMORY_LIMIT=8192
requested_allocation_mib=6144
allocation_succeeded_mib=6144

Observe memory while both Pods remain active

./run.sh metrics

The gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes metric attributes memory by Pod and GPU UUID. The observed 6,394 MiB (about 6.24 GiB) per Pod exceeds the probe’s 6,144 MiB allocation by 250 MiB. Metrics can include CUDA context and runtime overhead. This experiment does not measure that breakdown. Retain workload identity and request, limit, and usage values together when monitoring the shared device.

Measured per-Pod metric series

gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes{
  gpu_uuid="<same-gpu-uuid>",
  namespace="runai-fractioning-test",
  pod="fraction-8gi-a"} 6.704594944e+09

gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes{
  gpu_uuid="<same-gpu-uuid>",
  namespace="runai-fractioning-test",
  pod="fraction-8gi-b"} 6.704594944e+09

Step 9: Verify rejection above the limit

Run the following command to test an allocation that exceeds the 8 GiB contract:

./run.sh limit

This command removes the positive-test Pods and creates one Pod with an 8 GiB contract that attempts a 9 GiB allocation. The probe reports:

Measured over-limit result

NVIDIA_GPU_MEMORY_LIMIT=8192
requested_allocation_mib=9216
allocation_failed=out of memory

Measured negative-test Pod status

NAME                      READY   STATUS      NODE
fraction-8gi-over-limit   0/1     Completed   <gpu-node>

Here, cudaMalloc returns an out-of-memory error, which the probe handles before exiting with code 0. Completed is expected, not OOMKilled. This demonstrates allocation rejection, not container termination or general fault isolation.

Step 10: Clean up

Capture the VPC ID before deleting the cluster. The independent checks that follow use the default cluster name and Region. Substitute your configured values if you changed them.

Capture the VPC ID

VPC_ID=$(aws eks describe-cluster \
  --name runai-fractioning-blog --region us-east-2 \
  --query cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.vpcId --output text)

Remove the disposable environment

./run.sh cleanup

Standard cleanup removes the test namespace, Helm releases, and disposable cluster while preserving the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot.

Verify resource deletion

aws eks describe-cluster \
  --name runai-fractioning-blog --region us-east-2
aws cloudformation describe-stacks \
  --stack-name eksctl-runai-fractioning-blog-cluster \
  --region us-east-2
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --vpc-ids "$VPC_ID" --region us-east-2

Expect explicit resource-not-found responses for deleted resources. Authentication or permission errors do not establish deletion. Also inspect remaining node groups and cluster-tagged instances. If cleanup fails, inspect CloudFormation events and resolve owned dependencies before retrying. An absent Amazon EKS endpoint does not prove that its VPC is gone.

Use ./run.sh cleanup-all only when the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot are no longer needed. If image deletion is refused, confirm the AMI ID and sample ownership tag. Do not bypass the safeguard.

Production considerations

Treat this as a behavior validation. Use trusted workloads and apply least-privilege IAM, namespace controls, approved images, and admission rules for fraction requests. Choose whole GPUs or MIG on supported hardware when stronger isolation is required.

The pinned fractioning daemons use privileged containers, host PID access, and NRI/MPS host mounts. Restrict their deployment and configuration to trusted administrators.

Allow headroom for CUDA contexts, caches, batching, and runtime overhead. Measure latency and throughput under concurrent load. Monitor allocation failures, MPS health, NRI connectivity, and GPU errors. Pin the base AMI, driver, toolkit, device plugin, operator, scheduler, and workload images as one tested combination. Rebuild images and test rollback before rollout.

This walkthrough requires pre-provisioned GPU capacity. It does not configure or validate GPU-fraction-aware autoscaling. The fractional Pods select kai-scheduler, request no nvidia.com/gpu resource, and use a nodeSelector that targets a node group fixed at one node. Karpenter support for secondary schedulers is an open feature request (issue #742 on GitHub). The custom image cannot run on Amazon EKS Auto Mode-managed nodes, because Auto Mode selects and manages their AMI. A cluster can mix Auto Mode-managed nodes with managed node groups, but we did not validate this walkthrough in such a cluster.

Teams that use Karpenter can reference the same custom AMI by ID in an EC2NodeClass. The autoscaling limit still applies. We did not validate this path.

KAI Scheduler is a second scheduler. It handles queueing and placement for Pods that select it. If you already use Kueue, decide which component owns queueing for GPU workloads before you adopt KAI Scheduler.

We recommend running the Amazon EKS node monitoring agent on GPU nodes. In a November 18, 2026 regression run, the agent ran on the custom R615 image with MPS sharing active and reported healthy GPU conditions throughout the sharing and limit tests. That run did not test fault detection. Because GPU Operator already runs a Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) host engine, configure the agent to use that host engine instead of its bundled one.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to configure GPU-memory fractioning on Amazon EKS with a custom AL2023 image, using G5/A10G as the validated example. The approach extends to compatible NVIDIA GPUs after checking prerequisites and validating the selected configuration. You established the whole-GPU baseline, ran two bounded workloads on the same GPU, inspected per-Pod memory usage, and verified rejection of an allocation above the limit. Fractioning can improve access to existing capacity when workload memory fits. Production adoption also requires isolation controls and performance testing.

To repeat the experiment, clone the AWS Samples repository and compare your results with its validated evidence. Explore the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation and the Amazon EKS accelerated AMI guidance before adapting the example to your workloads.

The content and opinions in this post are those of the third-party author and AWS is not responsible for the content or accuracy of this post.

item.title: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Cust…
item.description: Full title: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization

Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a company’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone. For businesses, the value is twofold. A fine-tuned model delivers measurably better accuracy on domain-specific work while reducing costs: a smaller specialized model can match or exceed a frontier model on your task at a fraction of the per-token inference price. Those savings compound across millions of requests. Fine-tuning has therefore become an essential process for businesses looking to get more value from LLMs at lower costs.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters. LoRA aims to strike a balance between efficiency and expressiveness, however, the low-rank nature of the weight update inherently limits the representation power of LoRA fine-tuned models, potentially compromising performance on complex tasks. This trade-off hampers the ability of LoRA methods to capture complex patterns needed for diverse tasks. To address these challenges, Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) updates model parameters simultaneously, overcoming the low-rank limitations so LLMs can fully absorb complex domain-specific knowledge.

Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT), so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure. There is no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration required. In this post, we explore when and where FFT consistently outperforms LoRA across key benchmarks, examine the spectral properties of model weight matrices that explain this quality gap, provide practical hyperparameter tuning guidelines backed by controlled experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and show you how to get started with FFT on SageMaker AI.

Full Fine-Tuning: Why it matters

Model customization types like LoRA reduce trainable parameters by freezing the pre-trained model’s weights and injecting small, separate pairs of replacement matrices (called low-rank matrices) into the model layers. This works well for simple adaptations, but the low-rank structure inherently limits the representation power of the fine-tuned model. As tasks grow more complex and datasets scale beyond tens of thousands of examples, LoRA hits an accuracy plateau where increasing rank (and thus trainable parameters) fails to bridge the accuracy gap with standard fine-tuning. This plateau reveals that the performance gap isn’t simply because of fewer parameters. It’s caused by rank deficiency itself. The low-rank update can’t capture the full complexity of the weight changes needed for deep task adaptation.

However, for complex tasks and domains where large, good-quality datasets exist, full-rank fine-tuning excels by updating model parameters simultaneously. FFT modifies the model’s weight matrix uniformly, using the full representational capacity of the model’s weight matrices rather than restricting updates to a small subspace, and without introducing the abrupt, localized distortions characteristic of low-rank methods. The result is stronger model convergence, better activation alignment across model layers, and a model that faithfully captures both the target task distribution and the richness of its pre-trained knowledge. FFT’s quality advantage grows with dataset scale: at 100K+ training examples, FFT achieved 90.0 percent on LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness across code generation tasks, as shown in the following chart.

Figure 1: LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness by training method as training data scales to 100K+ examples

Furthermore, the following radar chart provides a holistic view: the base model (inner polygon) shows consistently low scores across all axes. LoRA (middle polygon) shows strong, balanced improvement. FFT (outer polygon) extends further on every dimension, with particularly pronounced leads on BLEU and ROUGE-2 scores. This multi-dimensional quality lead confirms that it isn’t a metric-specific artifact but a fundamental advantage of full-rank optimization.

Figure 2: Radar chart comparing the base model, LoRA, and FFT across quality dimensions

The details of how we arrived at these results, the coding datasets used for model customization, and the experimentation process are explained in detail in the following sections.

Experimentation and benchmark results

In this post we used the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) technique on a Qwen3-4B base model offered within Amazon SageMaker AI Studio and performed all the fine-tuning experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization across LoRA and FFT training methods. Within each experiment, both methods received the same prompts, targets, and evaluation code.

Dataset: Code generation 110K instruction pairs

For all the experimentation, we fine-tuned the Qwen3-4B base model on the Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset, a curated corpus of 110,000 coding instruction-response pairs spanning algorithm design, debugging, data structures, and systems programming. We applied a 90/5/5 split to the dataset: 99,000 records for training, 5,500 for validation to monitor convergence and training loss during the customization job, and 5,500 reserved as a held-out test set for unbiased evaluation of the final model, as registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets and shown in the following figure.

Figure 3: The 110K instruction-pair dataset registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets

Serverless Model Customization job

All the model customization experiments in this post were performed on Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization. Serverless Model Customization on SageMaker AI lets data scientists and machine learning (ML) engineers focus on model fine-tuning without managing infrastructure or GPU capacity planning. You specify the base model, dataset, and hyperparameters, and the service handles compute allocation and checkpoint management automatically in a serverless fashion. The following code snippet shows one such experiment for launching a Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) job on Serverless Model Customization using the SageMaker Python SDK.

from sagemaker.train.sft_trainer import SFTTrainer
from sagemaker.train.common import TrainingType

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=base_model_id,
    training_type=TrainingType.FULL,
    model_package_group=model_package_group_name,
    training_dataset=training_dataset,
    validation_dataset=val_dataset,
    s3_output_path=output_path,
    sagemaker_session=sess,
    role=role,
)

# Configure hyperparameters as needed
trainer.hyperparameters.learning_rate = 2e-5
trainer.hyperparameters.global_batch_size = 8
trainer.hyperparameters.max_epochs = 2
trainer.hyperparameters.lr_warmup_steps_ratio = 0.1

trainer.train(wait=False)

The code triggers a serverless model customization job, shown in the following screenshot, with training performance metrics tracked in the job and viewable in the linked MLflow app.

Figure 4: Serverless model customization job with training metrics tracked in MLflow

Switching from Full Fine-Tuning to LoRA requires only one change: set TrainingType.FULL to TrainingType.LORA. The rest of the code remains identical:

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=base_model_id,
    training_type=TrainingType.LORA,  # ← only change
    model_package_group=model_package_group_name,
    training_dataset=training_dataset,
    validation_dataset=val_dataset,
    ...
)

Model evaluation and benchmarking

We tested the resulting customized models across three diverse evaluation methods built into SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization: LLM-as-Judge, PRIMECODE, and MMLU, shown in the following image. Each targets a different dimension of model quality: semantic correctness, code generation fidelity, and general knowledge retention. Together they provide a comprehensive picture of the model customization quality.

Figure 5: The three built-in evaluation methods in SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization

The LLM-as-Judge metric uses a frontier model (in this post, Amazon Nova Pro) as an automated evaluator that reads the model’s generated code alongside the original prompt and judges whether the solution is logically correct. On serverless model customization you can evaluate both the customized model alongside the base model, as shown in the following figure.

Figure 6: LLM-as-Judge evaluation comparing the customized model and the base model

PRIMECODE is a custom scorer evaluation that measures how closely the model’s generated code matches reference solutions using deterministic text-similarity metrics: BLEU (n-gram precision), ROUGE-1/2/L (recall-oriented overlap), and F1 (precision-recall balance). These metrics are fully reproducible, making them ideal for controlled ablation studies. We used PRIMECODE as our primary metric for surface-level code quality because it quantifies how well the model has learned the coding patterns, formatting conventions, and implementation style present in the training data. A high BLEU score means the model generates code that looks structurally similar to expert-written solutions, as shown in the following results.

Figure 7: PRIMECODE text-similarity scores for the customized model

MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is a built-in benchmark that tests the model across 57 academic subjects from abstract algebra and anatomy to Nutrition and Philosophy. It measures whether the model retains its broad general knowledge after domain-specific fine-tuning, as shown in the following figure. We used MMLU as our forgetting detection guardrail. Fine-tuning on code can overwrite general capabilities stored in the model’s weights. By tracking MMLU accuracy before and after fine-tuning, we can quantify exactly how much general knowledge the model sacrifices for code generation improvement, and whether our hyperparameter choices accelerate or mitigate this trade-off.

Figure 8: MMLU accuracy before and after fine-tuning

Rapid experimentation at scale

The ease of setup and use of SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization let us perform rapid experimentation without re-provisioning infrastructure. We changed training types between LoRA and FFT, swept hyperparameters, and tested across multiple base models. Over a short time window, we ran tens of model customization experiments across multiple supported base models (Qwen3-4B, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, Nemotron-30B, Gemma-4-26B), systematically ablating learning rate, batch size, warmup ratio, epoch count, and dataset scale. Each experiment, from job submission to evaluation results, completed in a few hours and the resulting fine-tuned models were automatically registered in SageMaker Model Registry as versioned Model Packages, ready for review or deployment.

Hyperparameter options

SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization supports many hyperparameters. In this section, we explain a few important ones, informed by the series of experiments that we ran across multiple hyperparameter configurations within the previously mentioned code generation task. While effective values will vary by task, the patterns observed across these experiments provide useful starting points when configuring FFT model customization jobs. For more information about the hyperparameters that you can configure before launching an FFT model customization job, see the hyperparameters documentation page.

1. learning_rate

In full fine-tuning, the learning rate controls how aggressively every weight is updated. Unlike LoRA, where only small adapter matrices change, an FFT learning rate that is too high permanently overwrites pretrained knowledge. In our experiments, the following LR × dataset-size risk map shows that an LR of 2e-5 on a large dataset (over 100 thousand) was the safe zone.

Figure 9: Learning rate and dataset-size risk map for full fine-tuning

2. max_epochs

Epoch count in FFT is fundamentally a forgetting question, not a loss-curve question. Training loss will keep falling and your held-out validation will look healthy because it shares a distribution with training data, but capabilities on everything you didn’t train on quietly degrade. The LLM-as-Judge correctness score rose to 90.0 percent at 3 epochs, and extending beyond 3 epochs degraded every variant we experimented with.

3. global_batch_size

Batch size determines how many examples contribute to each gradient step. At a fixed learning rate, smaller batches produce more noisy updates that behave much like a higher learning rate, increasing forgetting risk. Larger batches reduce noise but also reduce the number of optimization steps, potentially underfitting.

Figure 10: Effect of global batch size on model quality

Catastrophic forgetting risk

FFT modifies every parameter in the model, including the parameters that encode general knowledge acquired during pre-training. When fine-tuning pushes these parameters too aggressively toward a narrow domain, the model can “forget” its broader capabilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. We tested for this systematically using MMLU, measuring general knowledge retention across all our fine-tuning configurations. A baseline configuration with warmup=5 percent, batch size 8, and LR=2e-5 best preserved general knowledge (MMLU), as shown in the following figure.

Figure 11: MMLU general-knowledge retention across hyperparameter configurations

Hence, it is important to note that FFT isn’t universally superior to LoRA, and its effectiveness is extremely sensitive to hyperparameter choices. For example, in our experiments, both FFT and LoRA underperformed the base model on MATH exact match, underscoring the challenge of preserving reasoning capabilities during domain-specific fine-tuning. Aggressive learning rates (LR ≥ 5e-5) in FFT proved particularly destructive, causing MATH scores to plummet to 2–3 percent and MMLU accuracy to drop to 3.6 percent, clear evidence of catastrophic forgetting. Additionally, LoRA slightly outperformed FFT on the LLM-as-Judge metric (81.5 percent compared to 79.5 percent), demonstrating that parameter-efficient methods can still hold an edge on subjective quality assessments. These findings reinforce that the choice between FFT and LoRA should be guided by careful experimentation, dataset characteristics, and a clear understanding of the trade-offs involved.

Conclusion

With Full Fine-Tuning on Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, your model can fully absorb domain-specific knowledge when task complexity and data scale demand it. If your use case requires deep adaptation, such as specialized reasoning, code generation, or domain-specific language understanding, and you have sufficient high-quality training data, FFT delivers measurably stronger results.

You can get started with FFT on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization with serverless training, built-in evaluation, and without infrastructure or compute capacity planning, so you can focus on your data and hyperparameter choices. You can use the SageMaker Python SDK to configure and launch your training and evaluation jobs programmatically. You can see the documentation for supported base models available for Full Fine-Tuning on Serverless Model Customization.

About the author

item.title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of…
item.description: Full title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips

At Exa, we are building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. We optimize the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. We use multi-tower semantic machine learning (ML) models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space, so users can express complex queries in natural language alongside traditional keyword search. The keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database. It must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. The unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything we do. At the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding the hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar isn’t a tuning detail. Any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number.

This post details how we optimized our embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware (AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2), and how an agentic development workflow drove the optimization.

Inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline, but it must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving.

Figure 1: A simplified view of the Exa stack

Every structured web document we rank as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. This figure shows how raw web data moves from Crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of Parse, Moderate and filter, then Embed, with the result served from a vector database.

Embedding documents at scale

Our experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding our existing corpus. We selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. A migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate our hardware choices.

Figure 2: The doubled inference load from the backfill

The preceding figure shows two parallel pipelines sharing the crawl and parse stages, one embedding with the live model into the live index and one re-embedding priority documents with the new model into the new index, which is what doubles the load. This doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider our hardware and optimization choices.

Optimization journey

AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance (inf2.xlarge), with one chip and two NeuronCores. Our workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so we run Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving us container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. The same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Our initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model. From that baseline, it became a march to push throughput (docs/sec) as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. The following chart shows the throughput gains at each milestone.

Figure 3: Throughput improvement across optimization milestones

Starting from the naive compile, a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement. The first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. We also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. The downcast outputs met our correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference (see Agentic methodology), so the accuracy impact was within our acceptance threshold.

NKI kernels

The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) library provides optimized kernels for common model layers and operations. These pre-built kernels deliver immediate gains on common features, and we used them to quickly remove the most straightforward sources of inefficiency. A drop-in attention kernel gave us the next bump in performance.

Memory layout optimization: A fused SwiGLU MLP kernel

The next bottleneck was memory spill. Profiles from the Neuron Explorer consistently showed large amounts of spill and reload from high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which kept the Tensor Engine from being fully utilized through the forward pass. Using a drop-in MLP kernel as a steppingstone to profile the shortcomings of the pre-built implementation, we wrote a custom weight-stationary fused SwiGLU MLP kernel that eliminated the HBM stalls.

We used the higher-level NKI language for layout operations, loops, and memory operations, and only dropped into the lower-level NKI ISA for specific tensor operations. Keeping most of the kernel in the higher-level language makes it more understandable for engineers, and easier to debug.

FLOPS reduction

At this point we hit a wall. Per-accelerator throughput measured with the other on-chip core idle was significantly higher than what we saw with both cores running simultaneously. That gap meant our theoretical data-parallel throughput should have been well above our realized aggregate performance, which pointed to contention between the cores.

Profiling and experimentation showed that our workload wasn’t yet saturating the Tensor Engine. The remaining headroom was ours to claim by making the computation leaner. The clearest path left was to reduce the overall FLOPS needed to produce our results by eliminating waste. We rewrote the attention kernel around the exact shapes in our model to cut FLOPS spent on padding. This is where kernel customization really paid off. Generic kernels are built to handle any shape, so they can’t take advantage of the specific shapes in a given architecture. We wrung more performance out of attention by tailoring the implementation to the real shape of our model’s head architecture. We also folded attention operations into single matmuls where the generic kernel used multiple instruction steps. That cut the inner-loop operations needed to compute the same values, which reduced HBM round trips and produced the final significant speedup.

In total, our final version was a 47% improvement in performance and cost per 1 million documents embedded, against our initial baseline.

Agentic methodology

Agents developed all of these optimizations inside a simple three part harness that lets them verify correctness, measure performance and profile the workload to find the next direction. Using Flyte, an ML ops workflow platform, each agent runs its own workflow. The workflow compiles a NEFF Neuron executable and checks a forward pass against a baseline dataset, which must reach 0.999 cosine similarity to the canonical model. It then profiles one forward pass and runs a 30 minute saturation benchmark on real hardware.

The harness supports agents at different costs. Lightweight models handle tedious work like grid searching compiler parameters, and correctness checks prevent drift. Reasoning agents test complex hypotheses and find bottlenecks, while the strongest code generators write custom kernels to fix them. Matching each agent to its task keeps costs in check, and validation keeps capable agents from drifting. Because many agents don’t know the latest features and syntax, neuron agentic development skills also helped.

The benefits of flexible compute

So far, we have optimized Inferentia2 for the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), but tuning one hardware family in one Region has hard limits. Spot and on demand availability vary by Region, and organizations with many consumers compete with themselves. Locking into one Region or instance type almost guarantees a compute shortage, and possibly degraded service.

Exa schedules compute across multiple Regions from one Kubernetes control plane. Our scheduler compares performance per dollar across instance types and packs pods onto the cheapest nodes, rescheduling as embedding demand shifts. Each hardware type we optimize for brings us closer to the global optimum. This is why our Inferentia2 work carried over directly to Trainium2. Shifting hardware profiles lets us free up nodes other teams need or absorb their unused reserved compute. For a long lived model, optimizing across hardware pays off enormously.

Conclusion

At the scale Exa operates, extracting maximum cost-performance from a flexible pool of hardware is what matters. Adding Neuron hardware to that pool and optimizing it with NKI has proven to be a major source of long-term cost savings.

About the authors

item.title: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure ch…
item.description: Full title: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin. Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training. Today, we’re introducing workload recovery and infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads.

SageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware. These features look at one node’s hardware at a time. They can’t tell whether the GPUs train correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the Kubernetes components a job depends on are working.

In this post, we walk through the three new capabilities that catch these failures. For each one, we show how to set it up and what it reports when it finds a problem:

  • MultiNodeTrainingValidation is a new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time.
  • The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
  • Hung job detection finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it.

Why node health alone isn’t enough

The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors. The InstanceStress deep health check runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices. The InstanceConnectivity check runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium. Together, these confirm that each node’s hardware works. They don’t show whether the GPUs compute correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the cluster’s Kubernetes components are healthy. Three kinds of failure get past them:

  • Numerical faults – A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run. Meta attributed 6 of the 419 unexpected interruptions in its 54-day Llama 3 405B pre-training run to silent data corruption (The Llama 3 Herd of Models).
  • Hung jobs – An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log.
  • Cluster-level failures – Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. HMA checks each node on its own, so it doesn’t see these problems. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it.

Solution overview

Each capability covers a different point in a training run. MultiNodeTrainingValidation runs when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirms that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the cluster continuously and, when a job fails, reports the pods and nodes that were involved. The following table summarizes the three.

CapabilityWhat it catchesWhen it runsAvailable on
MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health checkNaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time, on GPUs that pass hardware checksWhen instances are created or updated, or on demandEKS clusters, on supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instances
HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring AgentNode condition changes, pod and DaemonSet failures, and failed training jobs, with the pods and nodes involved. NCCL communication state for jobs that opt inContinuouslyEKS clusters
Hung job detectionJobs that stop making progress but don’t exitWhile each job runsSlurm clusters

Hung job detection is new for Slurm clusters. On EKS clusters, HyperPod already detects hung jobs that run through the HyperPod training operator, and Ray Train jobs get hang detection by default. We describe both options in the hung job detection section.

Each capability targets a different source of lost goodput. Scheduling goodput is the share of time that all the resources a job needs are available. Runtime goodput is the share of that time in which the job makes forward progress. Program goodput is the share of the hardware’s peak performance that the job gets. The following table shows the effect of each capability.

CapabilityScheduling goodputRuntime goodputProgram goodput
MultiNodeTrainingValidationInstances that fail the training test are labeled and, with automatic node recovery, replaced, so jobs don’t start on hardware that produces invalid outputFewer production runs lost to NaN or infinite loss from a faulty GPUFlags instances whose training doesn’t finish within the time limit
HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring AgentReports nodes that lose GPUs or EFA devices, missing device plugins, and taints, so you can restore capacity soonerNames the pods and nodes behind a failed job, so you find the cause and restart soonerNo direct effect
Hung job detectionNo direct effectFlags a hung job in minutes instead of hours, and can cancel it so Slurm requeues itNo direct effect

Consider a pre-training job running on 32 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs). If the job hangs at 1:00 AM and no one notices until 9:00 AM, it wastes 256 instance-hours or 2,048 GPU-hours. At the SageMaker HyperPod on-demand price of approximately $66 per instance-hour in US East (N. Virginia), the hang costs about $16,900. With a 15-minute hung job detection rule, HyperPod cancels the stalled job and Slurm requeues it. The hang costs about $530 instead, saving approximately $16,400.

Validate training correctness with the MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check

The MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check trains a fixed, known-good workload, first on each instance and then across instances. It catches GPUs that pass InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity but produce NaN or infinite loss once they train together. If an instance fails, HyperPod labels it as failed and, with automatic node recovery turned on, reboots or replaces it. When the check runs during provisioning, this happens before your jobs can use the instance.

How it works

MultiNodeTrainingValidation adds two tests to the deep health check run:

  • Tiny Megatron test: A short Megatron-LM training run on all GPUs of each instance.
  • Megatron test: The same workload across instances of the same type, communicating over EFA.

Either test fails an instance if the training loss becomes NaN or infinite, or if training doesn’t finish within the time limit. The workload is fixed, so a failure points to the hardware rather than to a model or code change.

The following table shows how it fits with the other deep health checks.

CheckWhat it runsWhat it catches
InstanceStressGPU and NVLink count, DCGM level 4 diagnostics, and EFA latency and bandwidth tests (Neuron tests on Trainium)Hardware that’s missing, failing, or unstable
InstanceConnectivityNCCL tests across GPU instances (NCCOM on Trainium)Slow or broken communication between instances
MultiNodeTrainingValidationTiny Megatron test on each instance, Megatron test across instancesGPUs that run but train incorrectly: NaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS.
  • An instance group of a supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instance type, such as ml.p5.48xlarge. The Megatron test runs across instances of the same type.

Turn on MultiNodeTrainingValidation for an instance group

HyperPod runs deep health checks when it creates or updates instances. To include MultiNodeTrainingValidation, add it to OnStartDeepHealthChecks in the instance group configuration that you pass to create-cluster or update-cluster. We turned on all three checks:

{
    "InstanceGroupName": "<instance-group>",
    "InstanceType": "ml.p5.48xlarge",
    "InstanceCount": 2,
    "LifeCycleConfig": {
        "SourceS3Uri": "s3://<bucket>/<prefix>",
        "OnCreate": "on_create.sh"
    },
    "ExecutionRole": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<hyperpod-execution-role>",
    "OnStartDeepHealthChecks": [
        "InstanceStress",
        "InstanceConnectivity",
        "MultiNodeTrainingValidation"
    ]
}

To confirm the setting, run the following command:

aws sagemaker describe-cluster \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --query "InstanceGroups[?InstanceGroupName=='<instance-group>'].OnStartDeepHealthChecks"

The output lists the three checks:

[
    [
        "InstanceStress",
        "InstanceConnectivity",
        "MultiNodeTrainingValidation"
    ]
]

Run MultiNodeTrainingValidation on demand

You can also check instances that are already in the cluster, for example before a long pre-training run. Use the StartClusterHealthCheck API:

aws sagemaker start-cluster-health-check \
    --cluster-name <cluster-name> \
    --deep-health-check-configurations \
    '[{"InstanceGroupName": "<instance-group>", "DeepHealthChecks": ["MultiNodeTrainingValidation"]}]'

To check specific instances instead of the whole group, add "InstanceIds": [...] to the configuration.

How long MultiNodeTrainingValidation takes

On our two-node cluster, the full deep health check took 1 hour 28 minutes after the instances finished their lifecycle scripts. DCGM level 4 diagnostics took most of that. The two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests added about 8 minutes. Instances can’t take workloads until the checks finish, so plan for this additional time when you add capacity.

TestCheckTime since previous result
HARDWARE_CHECKInstanceStress3 min
DCGM (level 4)InstanceStress74 min
EFAInstanceStress1 min
TINY_MEGATRONMultiNodeTrainingValidation4 min
NCCLInstanceConnectivity1 min
MEGATRON (2 instances)MultiNodeTrainingValidation4 min

Keep in mind that MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests the hardware with a fixed reference workload. A pass means the instances trained that workload correctly. It doesn’t guarantee that your own job will converge. We recommend running it on new capacity, on replacement instances, and before long pre-training runs.

Catch cluster-level failures with the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent

HMA watches the hardware on each node, but many failures that stop a training job happen in Kubernetes. A device plugin can crash-loop until its node stops offering GPUs to the scheduler, or a taint can evict a job’s pods. The job error rarely names the pod or node involved, so engineers piece together what happened from kubectl output, per-rank logs, and timestamps.

The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches these resources from one place in the cluster. When something breaks, it tells you what changed and which nodes, pods, and jobs are affected. It reports through Kubernetes events and structured CloudWatch logs. The agent only reports. It doesn’t reboot nodes or restart jobs, because the cause might be in the workload. HMA and HyperPod node recovery still handle hardware faults, and the HyperPod training operator still handles job restarts.

How the agent works

The agent runs as a single pod per cluster in the aws-hyperpod namespace and prefers CPU nodes, so it doesn’t use GPU capacity. It watches the following:

  • Nodes: The agent reports these changes: Condition changes such as NotReady or memory, disk, or PID pressure. Fewer allocatable GPUs or EFA devices. Lost NVIDIA capability labels. Added, changed, or removed taints. Missing HyperPod labels.
  • Critical infrastructure pods: DaemonSet pods in kube-system, aws-hyperpod, and kubeflow, plus the training operator’s controller. The agent reports crash loops, restarts, container errors, and pods that stay not ready.
  • DaemonSets: Required DaemonSets that are missing or have no available pods, rollouts that stall, and pods running on nodes that no longer allow them.
  • Training jobs: HyperPodPyTorchJob, Kubeflow PyTorchJob (v1), and Kubeflow TrainJob (v2). When a job fails, the agent records the failure reason with the job’s pods and nodes.
  • NCCL communication: For jobs that opt in, the state of the job’s NCCL communicators, read from NCCL’s built-in reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem.

The agent reports what it finds in two places:

  • Kubernetes events on the affected node, pod, DaemonSet, or job. A Warning event marks a problem and a Normal event marks its recovery. You read them with kubectl get events and kubectl describe.
  • Structured JSON logs in the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, which keep the history after Kubernetes events expire.

The following table lists the events you’re most likely to see.

Event reasonRaised when
TrainingJobFailedA HyperPodPyTorchJob or Kubeflow job fails. The message includes the failure reason from the job’s operator.
CriticalPodCrashLoop, CriticalPodRestartedA device plugin, HMA, or another critical pod crash-loops or restarts.
NecessaryDaemonSetMissingA DaemonSet you declared as required is missing or has no available pods.
NodeResourceDegradedA node’s allocatable GPUs or EFA devices drop or disappear.
NodeConditionDegradedA node becomes NotReady or reports memory, disk, or PID pressure.
NodeTaintAdded, NoExecuteTaintAppliedA node is tainted. For a NoExecute taint, the log lists the pods and jobs that might be evicted.
DaemonSetMisscheduledDaemonSet pods are running on nodes that no longer allow them.
NodeRecovered, PodRecovered, DaemonSetRecoveredA problem reported earlier has cleared.

For the full list of events, see the documentation.

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS.
  • For an existing cluster, kubectl and Helm access to the cluster, and the HyperPod Helm chart from the sagemaker-hyperpod-cli repository.
  • NCCL 2.24 or later in the training container, if you want to monitor NCCL communication.

Install and verify the agent

If your cluster already uses the HyperPod Helm chart, apply the agent’s custom resource definition (CRD) first, because Helm doesn’t install CRDs during an upgrade. Then upgrade the release with the agent turned on:

git clone https://github.com/aws/sagemaker-hyperpod-cli.git
cd sagemaker-hyperpod-cli/helm_chart
helm dependencies update HyperPodHelmChart

kubectl apply \
    -f HyperPodHelmChart/charts/hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor/crds/

helm upgrade dependencies HyperPodHelmChart \
    --namespace kube-system \
    --reset-then-reuse-values \
    --set hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor.enabled=true \
    --set hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor.region=<region>

The upgrade also moves the other HyperPod components in the chart, such as HMA and the device plugins, to the chart’s current versions. To see what will change first, run the same command with --dry-run=server.

Check that the agent is running and that its health report exists:

kubectl get deployment \
    -n aws-hyperpod \
    hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitoring-agent

kubectl get hyperpodkrmaconfigs default -o yaml

The health report lists the HyperPod components that the agent tracks, such as HMA, and when their status last changed:

status:
  components:
    - name: DaemonSet/aws-hyperpod/health-monitoring-agent
      since: "2026-11-10T16:47:57Z"
      status: Healthy
      instances: []
  lastReportTime: "2026-11-10T17:19:36Z"

By default, HMA is the only required DaemonSet. If your cluster uses the device plugins from the HyperPod Helm chart, add them so that the agent reports a missing plugin. Also add the namespaces where your training jobs run, so that it can link pod failures to their jobs. Each list replaces its default, so keep the default entries. Save the following as krma-values.yaml:

hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor:
  monitoring:
    monitoredNamespaces:
      - aws-hyperpod
      - kube-system
      - default
      - kubeflow
      - ml-team-a
    necessaryDaemonsets:
      - name: health-monitoring-agent
        namespace: aws-hyperpod
      - name: dependencies-nvidia-device-plugin
        namespace: kube-system
      - name: dependencies-aws-efa-k8s-device-plugin
        namespace: kube-system

Then apply it:

helm upgrade dependencies HyperPodHelmChart \
    --namespace kube-system \
    --reset-then-reuse-values \
    -f krma-values.yaml

See what the agent reports

To see how the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent handles an infrastructure failure, we deployed a small DaemonSet into aws-hyperpod, pinned it to one node, and made it exit a few seconds after starting. It behaves like a crash-looping device plugin without touching the real one. Within seconds, the agent raised events on the pod and the DaemonSet:

kubectl get events -A \
    --field-selector source=hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitoring-agent

NAMESPACE TYPE REASON OBJECT MESSAGE
aws-hyperpod Warning CriticalPodRestarted pod/demo-plugin-4wsqw Critical infrastructure pod container crash restarted (count: 2)
aws-hyperpod Warning CriticalPodCrashLoop pod/demo-plugin-4wsqw Critical infrastructure pod container crash in CrashLoopBackOff
aws-hyperpod Warning DaemonSetMisscheduled daemonset/demo-plugin DaemonSet has 1 misscheduled pods

Next, we ran a two-node HyperPodPyTorchJob and made one rank exit during training. The agent raised a TrainingJobFailed event on the job:

NAMESPACE TYPE REASON OBJECT MESSAGE
ml-team-a Warning TrainingJobFailed hyperpodpytorchjob/llama-pretrain Training job HyperPod PyTorchJob failed:
Fault detected on training pod llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-nh5gb:
A training worker process has crashed: Local Rank 0 exited ...

It also wrote the failure to CloudWatch with the pods and nodes involved, so you don’t need to look them up from the job’s pod list:

{"level":"warn","msg":"=== Job Failure Detected ===","component":"HyperpodPyTorchJob",
"job":"llama-pretrain","namespace":"ml-team-a","type":"HyperPod PyTorchJob",
"reason":"Fault detected on training pod llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-nh5gb: A training worker process has crashed ..."}
{"level":"warn","msg":"Affected Pods","component":"HyperpodPyTorchJob",
"pods":["llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-nh5gb","llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-f9dmg"]}
{"level":"warn","msg":"Affected Nodes","component":"HyperpodPyTorchJob",
"nodes":["hyperpod-i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001","hyperpod-i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002"]}

The agent writes these logs to the cluster log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>, in streams named SageMakerClusterMonitoringAgent/<instance-group>/<instance-id>. It starts a new stream when it moves to another node, so filter by the stream prefix. For sample queries, see the documentation.

Monitor NCCL communication for a job

NCCL 2.24 and later include the reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem, a small listener in each NCCL process that reports the state of the job’s communicators. For jobs that opt in, the agent reads this report from every pod every 30 seconds.

By default, NCCL binds the RAS listener to localhost inside the pod, where the agent can’t reach it. To opt a job in, you bind the listener to the pod IP instead. That makes port 28028 reachable on the pod network, which NVIDIA’s documentation notes has security implications. Before you turn it on, apply a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that allows TCP port 28028 only from the agent’s pod and still allows traffic between the job’s own pods. The agent’s documentation includes an example policy. Then set NCCL_RAS_ADDR in the training container:

apiVersion: sagemaker.amazonaws.com/v1
kind: HyperPodPyTorchJob
...
containers:
  - name: pytorch
    env:
      - name: POD_IP
        valueFrom:
          fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.podIP}
      - name: NCCL_RAS_ADDR # set only after the NetworkPolicy is in place
        value: "$(POD_IP):28028"

To confirm the setting, turn on NCCL debug logging with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,RAS. Each rank then logs the address RAS listens on:

[default3]:llama-pretrain-workers-6c7f5bb445-gxnsf:129:203 [3] NCCL INFO RAS client listening socket at 10.0.1.11<28028>

If the address is ::1 or 127.0.0.1, NCCL_RAS_ADDR isn’t set and the agent can’t reach the listener.

For each monitored job, the agent combines the per-pod results into a job-level state. The job is healthy when every pod returns a valid report, degraded when only some do, and unhealthy when none do. Unhealthy usually means the training processes have stopped.

The agent logs a summary after each polling cycle. In a run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances, every cycle reported both training pods healthy, 30 seconds apart:

{"level":"info","timestamp":"2026-11-12T07:14:27.163Z","msg":"NCCL RAS monitoring cycle completed","component":"nccl-ras-informer-llama-pretrain","duration":4.00535305,"total_endpoints":2,"healthy":2,"failed":0,"overall_status":"healthy"}

The agent also writes each RAS report to CloudWatch, so you can spot communicator problems while the job is still running. In our test, we made one rank of a two-node job stop calling all_reduce. The report from the next polling cycle showed the communicator out of step and named the rank, GPU, process, and node that had fallen behind:

Group Comms Nodes Ranks Ranks Ranks Status Errors
# in group per comm per node per comm in group
0 1 2 1 2 2 RUNNING MISMATCH

#0-0 (2958ae23ccc57a88) MISMATCH
Communicator ranks have different AllReduce operation counts
Rank 0 has launched up to operation 3078 -- GPU 0 managed by process 473 on node 10.0.1.11
Rank 1 has launched up to operation 3077 -- GPU 0 managed by process 474 on node 10.0.2.22

Rank 1 is one operation behind rank 0, so start with rank 1’s GPU on node 10.0.2.22.

Detect and recover hung jobs on HyperPod Slurm clusters

A training job can hang without exiting. An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can leave the job holding its GPUs while Slurm still shows it as running. It stays that way until someone notices that the loss or the log has stopped changing. Teams that run Slurm often build their own watchdog scripts and alarms to catch these jobs, and then need to maintain them.

Today, we’re launching hung job detection for SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters. It finds these jobs, writes an event to CloudWatch, and can cancel a hung job so that Slurm puts it back in the queue. You turn it on for each job with an environment variable that points to a small rules file. It needs no changes to your training scripts or containers, and it works with PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and custom scripts.

How hung job detection works

Hung job detection runs as an agent on every node and is off by default. The agent watches only jobs that set the HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES environment variable to the path of a rules file. The rules file decides how the agent detects a hang:

  • Default detection watches the job’s standard output and GPU activity. It declares a hang when the output stops for an extended period while the GPUs sit idle but still hold memory. That’s what a rendezvous hang looks like, when one node fails and the others wait at a barrier. It also declares a hang when the output stops for a longer period, whatever the GPUs are doing. In our test, the first case fired 15 minutes after the job’s last output.
  • Custom rules watch your log for regular expressions that you choose. A progress rule declares a hang when a line such as your training step message doesn’t appear within its timeout. An error rule declares a hang as soon as a line such as an NCCL error appears. Custom rules replace default detection for that job.
Default detectionCustom rules
Turn on with{“enabled”: true}One or more enabled log_pattern rules
Declares a hang whenOutput stops while GPUs are idle but hold memory, or output stops for a longer periodA progress pattern doesn’t appear within its timeout, or an error pattern appears
MissesJobs that keep their GPUs busy without making progress, such as a job stuck in a loopHangs your patterns don’t describe. If a pattern keeps matching, no hang is declared, even with idle GPUs

When the agent declares a hang, it writes a HANG_DETECTED event to CloudWatch. If the rules file sets the action to cancel, the agent also cancels the job and Slurm requeues it. With the default action, notify, the agent writes the event and leaves the job running.

Hung job detection is separate from auto-resume, which restarts jobs that exit after a hardware failure. Auto-resume handles jobs that crash and hung job detection handles jobs that keep running without making progress.

On HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, HyperPod already detects hung jobs in two cases. The HyperPod training operator checks the logs of each HyperPodPyTorchJob against rules in the job specification and restarts the job when it hangs. The same rules can also restart a job whose throughput drops or whose loss spikes. You don’t need Ray for this. For Ray Train jobs, HyperPod hung job detection for Ray watches every worker by default, with no changes to your code.

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Slurm.
  • A HyperPod Slurm AMI released on or after November 10, 2026, which includes hung job detection. Clusters created on or after that date already have it. To check an existing cluster without updating it, run srun --help on a cluster node. If the output lists --no-hang-detection, the cluster supports hung job detection. If it doesn’t, update the cluster software first. The update replaces each instance’s root volume, so back up anything stored there before you update.
  • A rules file that every compute node in the job can read at the same path. The agent reads the file from that path on each node. Shared storage such as Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is a straightforward option. To keep rules files in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), copy them to the same path on every node, for example in your lifecycle script. If you plan to use a directory such as /opt/slurm, first confirm that it’s shared across nodes rather than local to each one.

Turn on hung job detection

Create a rules file on shared storage. The smallest valid file turns on default detection:

echo '{"enabled": true}' > /fsx/my-project/rules.json
chmod 600 /fsx/my-project/rules.json

The agent uses whatever rules file a job points to and doesn’t check who owns it. Anyone who can edit the file, or replace it in its directory, can change detection for every job that uses it, including making the agent cancel those jobs. The chmod 600 in the example keeps a personal rules file private to its owner. For a file that a team shares, use chmod 644 so the team can read it and only its maintainer can edit it. In both cases, make the parent directory writable only by its owner so nobody can swap the file.

Then point the job at the rules file when you submit it:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=llama-pretrain
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --export=ALL,HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES=/fsx/my-project/rules.json

srun python train.py

To use one rules file for many jobs, you can also set HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES in a shell profile or a site-wide profile script.

When a monitored job starts, the first lines of its output show that the agent registered it:

[Auto Resume] Info: [hang_detection] Exported stdout path for job 1: /fsx/my-project/llama-pretrain-1.out
[Auto Resume] Info: [hang_detection] Registered job step: job=1 step=0 node=ip-10-1-40-47

These lines also appear when the rules file is invalid, so check CloudWatch for a CONFIG_ERROR event too, as described in the next section.

Add custom rules to track training progress

Default detection can’t catch a job that keeps its GPUs busy without making progress, so we recommend at least one rule that watches for your training steps or epochs. The following rules file cancels the job if no epoch finishes for 45 minutes, or as soon as an NCCL error appears:

{
    "enabled": true,
    "rules": [
        {
            "name": "epoch_progress",
            "type": "log_pattern",
            "enabled": true,
            "log_pattern": "Epoch \\d+/\\d+ complete",
            "start_timeout_minutes": 30,
            "timeout_minutes": 45,
            "stop_pattern": "Training complete"
        },
        {
            "name": "nccl_error",
            "type": "log_pattern",
            "enabled": true,
            "log_pattern": "NCCL error",
            "fault_on_match": true
        }
    ],
    "action_policy": {
        "action": "cancel"
    }
}

The fields work as follows:

  • Set enabled to true on each rule. Rules are off by default.
  • start_timeout_minutes is how long the job can run before the pattern first appears. Set it longer than the time your job needs to load the model, compile, and restore a checkpoint.
  • timeout_minutes is how long the pattern can stay absent after that. Set it longer than the biggest normal gap, including checkpoint saves and evaluation.
  • stop_pattern turns the rule off when it matches, so work after training ends isn’t flagged.
  • fault_on_match marks an error pattern. One match means the job is hung.

By default, the agent reads the job’s Slurm output file. To watch a different file, set monitoring.log_file. To cut false positives, set metric_evaluation_data_points on a rule so that several 10-second checks in a row must fail before the agent declares a hang. A rules file can have up to 20 rules and be up to 1 MB.

Start with "action": "notify" while you tune timeouts and patterns, and switch to cancel once the events match real hangs.

View hung job detection events in CloudWatch

HyperPod writes detection events from the controller node to the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>, in the stream SageMakerHangJobDetectionEvents/<controller-instance-group>/<controller-instance-id>. Events for every job land in this stream, whichever node the job ran on. To find the events for one job, filter by its job ID:

aws logs filter-log-events \
    --log-group-name /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id> \
    --log-stream-name-prefix SageMakerHangJobDetectionEvents/ \
    --filter-pattern '{ $.job_id = "12345" }'

We tested each detection method on a HyperPod Slurm cluster with two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. The first test job allocated GPU memory and then stopped producing output. Default detection flagged it 15 minutes after its last output:

{
    "time": "2026-11-12T16:49:36.39710952Z",
    "level": "INFO",
    "msg": "HANG_DETECTED",
    "event_type": "HANG_DETECTED",
    "job_id": "1",
    "step_id": "0",
    "node": "ip-10-1-40-47",
    "evidence": "stdout stale for 15 min and GPU idle with memory allocated",
    "layer": "signal_evaluator",
    "detected_at": "2026-11-12T16:49:36.378940227Z",
    "job_action": "notify",
    "config_source": "per_job_env_var"
}

The layer field shows which method fired: signal_evaluator for default detection, or pattern_evaluator for a custom rule. In a second test, a progress rule with a 2-minute timeout fired 2 minutes after the job’s last step. In a third, an error rule fired about one second after the job printed an NCCL error line. Because that rules file used cancel, the agent also wrote a HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event with the action Slurm took (we’ve left out the time, level, and msg fields):

{"event_type":"HANG_DETECTED","job_id":"3","step_id":"0","node":"ip-10-1-40-47","evidence":"rule \"nccl_error\": fault pattern matched immediately","layer":"pattern_evaluator","detected_at":"2026-11-12T16:34:41.870908329Z","job_action":"cancel","config_source":"per_job_env_var"}
{"event_type":"HANG_ACTION_TAKEN","job_id":"3","action":"requeue","node":"ip-10-1-40-47","instance_id":"i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001"}

Slurm put the job back in the queue, and the requeued run started about 2.5 minutes later. sacct shows both runs:

$ sacct --duplicates -X -j 3 --format=JobID,State,Restarts,Start,End
JobID State Restarts Start End
----------- --------- ------- ------------------- -------------------
3 REQUEUED 0 2026-11-12T16:34:25 2026-11-12T16:34:41
3 COMPLETED 1 2026-11-12T16:37:10 2026-11-12T16:37:26

Slurm requeues a job up to the cluster’s MaxBatchRequeue limit, which was 5 on our cluster. A job submitted with #SBATCH --no-requeue reported "action": "cancel" instead and stayed canceled. With notify, there’s no HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event. The agent follows HANG_DETECTED with a record that says Hang notification sent, no automatic action taken.

If a rules file is missing or invalid, the agent doesn’t monitor the job and writes a CONFIG_ERROR event instead. Here’s the event for a rules file with a JSON syntax error:

{"event_type":"CONFIG_ERROR","job_id":"5","node":"ip-10-1-40-47","config_path":"/fsx/my-project/rules.json","error":"config file found but failed to load: load failed: invalid JSON in config file /fsx/my-project/rules.json: unexpected end of JSON input","message":"Hang detection rules file is invalid and will not be applied. Please fix the rules file and resubmit your job."}

The job ran to completion without monitoring, and nothing appeared in sbatch, squeue, or the job’s output. Test a new rules file with a short job and check for this event before you use it for production jobs.

With notify, the job keeps running until someone acts on the event. To get an alert, create a CloudWatch metric filter for HANG_DETECTED events and an alarm that notifies an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic:

aws logs put-metric-filter \
    --log-group-name /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id> \
    --filter-name hung-jobs \
    --filter-pattern '{ $.event_type = "HANG_DETECTED" }' \
    --metric-transformations \
    metricName=HungJobsDetected,metricNamespace=HyperPod/HungJobs,metricValue=1

Turn off hung job detection

To turn off detection for a job that would otherwise inherit HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES, add --no-hang-detection to srun, or to sbatch to cover every step in the job. To turn it off for every job that uses a rules file, set "enabled": false in the file. Running jobs keep their current settings, and the change applies to jobs you submit afterward.

srun --no-hang-detection python train.py

Conclusion

Node health is essential to reliable distributed training, but it does not provide a complete picture of workload health. MultiNodeTrainingValidation detects instances that pass hardware diagnostics but produce invalid training results. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent connects Kubernetes infrastructure failures to the jobs, pods, and nodes involved. Hung job detection identifies Slurm jobs that remain active after they stop making progress and can return them to the queue automatically.

Together, these capabilities help you detect failures earlier, shorten investigations, and raise goodput by reducing the GPU time spent on workloads that can’t make useful progress. Use MultiNodeTrainingValidation when adding or revalidating capacity, run the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent continuously on supported Amazon EKS clusters, and begin hung job detection in notify mode before you switch to automatic cancellation. To get started, see the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency documentation for Amazon EKS and the hung job detection documentation for Slurm. To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page.

The authors would like to thank Hengyu Lou, Vishal Shahane, Ziyao Huang, and Haard Mehta for their contributions to this post and features.

About the authors

item.title: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case.

Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model.

What is the JumpStart Model Leaderboard?

The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it shows two kinds of information:

  • Quality scores on three public benchmarks (BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro) that AWS runs itself, using the same evaluation setup for every model so the numbers are comparable.
  • Performance and cost metrics that AWS measures by sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint using each JumpStart deployment configuration, so you see how fast a model responds and what it costs to run.

Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time.

The following screenshot shows the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model.

Figure 1: Leaderboard overview in SageMaker Studio

Key concepts

This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves.

Quality benchmarks

A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs:

BenchmarkWhat it measures, in plain terms
BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)A set of challenging tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as logical deduction, tracking objects, and multi-step arithmetic.
GPQA DiamondGraduate-level science questions that are difficult to answer by searching the web. A good signal of deep reasoning.
MMLU-ProBroad knowledge and reasoning across many subjects, such as science, law, and engineering, using harder multiple-choice questions.

Higher is better for all three. The leaderboard shows each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark.

Use case profiles and optimization goals

Speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see:

  • Use case profile. Select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu. The default is Max Context. The profile changes only the performance and cost metrics. Quality benchmark scores are the same for every profile.
  • Optimization goal. For each profile, a model can have several deployment configurations, and the leaderboard shows metrics for one at a time. Choose which one with the Optimized for menu. The default is Balanced.

Each optimization goal picks a different configuration:

Optimization goalConfiguration shown
BalancedThe configuration with the lowest estimated cost per token. Because cost per token depends on both instance price and throughput, this balances what you pay per hour against how fast the instance generates tokens.
Cost optimizedThe configuration with the lowest hourly instance price. Latency can be higher and throughput lower than with other goals.
Latency optimizedThe configuration with the lowest time to first token.
Throughput optimizedThe configuration with the highest throughput. These configurations can use speculative decoding.

Performance metrics

MetricWhat it tells you
Time to first token (TTFT)How long a user waits before the model starts responding. Lower is better, and it matters most for chat.
Throughput per request (tokens/s)How many tokens the model generates per second. Higher is better, and it matters for batch and high-volume workloads.
Instance cost ($/hr)The estimated cost per hour given a specified instance type.

A note on cost: Estimated cost reflects SageMaker instance cost only, based on the on-demand hourly rate for the configuration’s default instance type. It does not include data transfer, storage, inference component costs, or discounts such as Reserved Instances or AWS Savings Plans. Your actual bill will vary. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator for billing estimates.

How we benchmark

Published benchmark scores often come from different teams using different prompts, settings, and hardware, which makes them hard to compare. We took a different approach:

  • One method for every model. AWS runs each benchmark with the same evaluation harness and settings across all models on the leaderboard.
  • Measured on SageMaker. Performance and cost come from sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint deployed with each JumpStart deployment configuration, the same configurations you can launch.

For full details, including prompts, generation settings, and how configurations are measured, see JumpStart model leaderboard benchmarks.

Walkthrough: Finding a model

The following steps show how to go from browsing to a deployed model. You need access to SageMaker Studio and permission to deploy JumpStart models.

Step 1: Open the leaderboard

In SageMaker Studio, open the Models page, then select the Leaderboard view. The leaderboard keeps the same search bar and filters as the other views, and it has its own URL. You can bookmark it or share a direct link with your team.

The following screenshot shows the Models page with the Leaderboard view selected.

Figure 2: JumpStart base models page with the Leaderboard view selected

Step 2: Narrow the list with filters

Use the same search and filters you already use elsewhere in JumpStart to keep only the models that fit your requirements. Common filters include license, provider, and input and output modality. Start with hard requirements, for example a license that allows commercial use, before you look at scores.

The following screenshot shows the leaderboard filtered by input modality, output modality, and license.

Figure 3: Leaderboard with filters applied

Step 3: Choose a use case profile and optimization goal

Above the leaderboard, select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu (default: Max Context). Then choose a goal from the Optimized for menu (default: Balanced). For a chatbot your customers interact with, Latency optimized is a sensible start. For overnight document processing, Throughput optimized or Cost optimized may fit better. The performance and cost columns update, and quality scores stay the same.

The following screenshots show the View benchmarks for your use case and Optimized for menus above the leaderboard.

Figure 4: View benchmarks for your use case menu

Figure 5: Optimized for menu

Step 4: Read the heatmap and customize columns

Each column has a blue heatmap, so the top-performing models stand out at a glance: the deeper the blue, the stronger the result in that column. Sort any benchmark column to rank models by the metric you care about most. Use the column settings (gear icon) to hide metrics you don’t need, and scroll horizontally to see more. The model name columns stay frozen as you scroll, and a fade at the edge shows when more columns are available.

The following screenshot shows the heatmap and the column settings menu.

Figure 6: Heatmap and column settings

Step 5: Deploy or customize the model

Choose a model to open it. From there, you have options to deploy the model or, for models that support serverless customization, to customize it. If you deploy, choose the same use case and optimization goal you compared on the leaderboard.
